_lisez_moi: Ce que les etoiles racontent dans Ton ciel (ligne 160). Fichier DERIVE : python etoiles/outils/infos.py. Ne pas corriger a la main.
origines : l'origine du nom d'une etoile nommee, par langue d'interface (catalogue de l'UAI, WGSN ; Kunitzsch & Smart 2006).

portraits : par figure, dans l'ordre de ses etoiles, « lettre,classe,rapport » : la lettre spectrale (OBAFGKM), la classe (sg supergeante, g geante, sous sous-geante, e etoile), le diametre rapporte au Soleil s'il est mesure (SIMBAD). Vide : type illisible.
textes : les gabarits du portrait par langue ; m / f : les six couleurs (bleu, blanc, jaune pale, jaune, orange, rouge) au genre de la classe (genre : sg g sous e).
histoires : la petite histoire de chaque figure, montree quand elle est complete (d'apres Ian Ridpath, Star Tales).

origines.Megrez: From Arabic: “the root of the Great Bear's tail”.

origines.Tejat: From Arabic: an old Arabic name of unknown meaning.

origines.Alhena: From Arabic: “the mark on the camel's neck (probable meaning)”.
origines.Betelgeuse: From Arabic: “the hand of al-Jawza (the giant Orion)”.
origines.Albireo: From Ancient Greek: a long garbling of the Greek ornis, “the bird”.
origines.Alcyone: From Ancient Greek: one of the seven Pleiades, daughters of Atlas.
origines.Atlas: From Ancient Greek: the Titan who holds up the sky, father of the Pleiades.
origines.Merope: From Ancient Greek: one of the seven Pleiades, daughters of Atlas.

histoires.ourse: For the Greeks, this is Callisto, a huntress turned into a bear. Zeus placed her in the sky. Her seven bright stars have always helped people find the Pole Star.
histoires.gemeaux: Castor and Pollux, two inseparable twins. When Castor died, Pollux, who was immortal, chose to share his immortality with him. Zeus united them forever in the sky.
histoires.orion: Orion was a giant hunter who boasted he could kill every animal. The Earth sent a scorpion that stung him. Since then, Orion and the Scorpion sit at opposite ends of the sky: when one rises, the other sets.
histoires.lyre: This is the lyre of Orpheus, the greatest musician in Greek mythology. Hermes had made it from a tortoise shell. Its music charmed animals, trees and even stones.
histoires.cygne: A swan flying along the Milky Way. For the Greeks, it is Zeus himself, disguised as a swan. It is also called the Northern Cross.
histoires.fleche: A little arrow, one of the smallest constellations in the sky. The Greeks saw it as the arrow Apollo shot at the Cyclopes, or one of Heracles' arrows.
histoires.pleiades: The seven daughters of the Titan Atlas. The hunter Orion chased them endlessly, so Zeus turned them into doves, then into stars. With the naked eye you can see six or seven, huddled together like a small family.
histoires.couronne: The crown of Ariadne, the princess who helped Theseus escape from the labyrinth. Abandoned on an island, she was comforted by the god Dionysus, who married her. He threw her crown into the sky, where its jewels became stars.
histoires.cocher: A charioteer holding a goat and her two kids. The Greeks saw him as Erichthonius, a king of Athens said to have invented the four-horse chariot. The goat is Capella, one of the brightest stars in the sky.
histoires.cassiopee: Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia, boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. To punish her, Poseidon sent a sea monster. In the sky she circles the pole, sometimes upside down.
histoires.cephee: Cepheus was king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. To save his land from the sea monster, he had to chain his daughter to a rock. His constellation looks like a house with a pointed roof.
histoires.corbeau: Apollo sent a crow to fetch water in a cup. The bird dawdled on the way, then lied to excuse itself. Apollo placed it in the sky, forever kept away from the nearby Cup.
histoires.dauphin: This dolphin found Amphitrite, the nymph the god Poseidon wanted to marry. To thank it, Poseidon placed it among the stars. It is a tiny diamond-shaped constellation.
histoires.pegase: Pegasus, the winged horse, was born from the blood of Medusa when Perseus cut off her head. The hero Bellerophon rode him to fight the Chimera. Four stars draw a great square: the horse's body.
histoires.croix: The smallest of the 88 constellations, and one of the most famous. European navigators of the 16th century carved it out of Centaurus. It points the way to the South Pole and appears on several flags.
histoires.petiteourse: A little bear whose tail ends with the Pole Star. Greek sailors used it to find north, long before the compass. The whole sky seems to turn around it.
histoires.lion: The Nemean lion, a monster whose skin was so tough that no weapon could pierce it. Heracles strangled it with his bare hands: it was the first of his twelve labours. Afterwards he wore its skin as armour.
histoires.taureau: Zeus turned himself into a magnificent white bull to carry off the princess Europa. He bore her on his back across the sea to Crete. In the sky only the front of the animal shows, as if it were still swimming.
histoires.bouvier: A herdsman who seems to drive the Great Bear around the pole. His brightest star, Arcturus, means “the guardian of the bear”. For some Greeks he is Arcas, the son of Callisto.
histoires.andromede: Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, was chained to a rock as an offering to a sea monster. The hero Perseus arrived at the last moment, freed her and married her. Among her stars hides the Andromeda Galaxy, visible to the naked eye.
histoires.persee: Perseus cut off the head of Medusa, whose gaze turned people to stone. On his way home he rescued Andromeda from the sea monster. In the sky he still holds Medusa's head, whose eye is the star Algol.
histoires.hercule: Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, the strongest hero in mythology. He carried out twelve impossible labours, such as killing the Nemean lion and the Lernaean Hydra. In the sky he kneels, one foot on the Dragon's head.
histoires.dragon: Ladon, the dragon that guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides. Heracles killed it to take the apples, and the goddess Hera placed it in the sky. It coils around the pole, between the two Bears.
histoires.aigle: The eagle of Zeus, which carried the king of the gods' thunderbolts. It also carried off young Ganymede to Mount Olympus. Its star Altair forms, with Vega and Deneb, the great Summer Triangle.
histoires.triangle: Three stars that look like the Greek letter delta (Δ). The Greeks saw in it the Nile Delta, or the island of Sicily. It is one of the easiest constellations to draw.
histoires.vierge: For the Greeks, she is Dike, the goddess of justice, or Demeter, the goddess of the harvest. She holds an ear of wheat: the star Spica. When people became wicked, justice left the Earth for the sky.
histoires.scorpion: The scorpion that stung the hunter Orion. The gods placed them at opposite ends of the sky, so that they would never meet again. Its heart is Antares, a star as red as the planet Mars.
histoires.sagittaire: A centaur, half man and half horse, aiming his bow at the Scorpion. For some Greeks he was Crotus, a hunting satyr, friend of the Muses. In his direction lies the centre of our galaxy.
histoires.grandchien: The dog of the hunter Orion, following him across the sky. It carries Sirius, the brightest star of the night. For other Greeks it is Laelaps, a dog so fast that no prey could escape it.
histoires.belier: The ram with the golden fleece, which saved two children, Phrixus and Helle, by carrying them through the air. Its fleece was guarded by a dragon, then taken by Jason and the Argonauts. Two thousand years ago, the Sun stood here at the start of spring.
histoires.cancer: The crab sent by the goddess Hera to bother Heracles during his fight with the Hydra. The hero crushed it with a kick. To thank it, Hera placed it in the sky, faint, with no bright star.
histoires.balance: The scales of justice, held by its neighbour, Virgo. For the Greeks these stars were the Scorpion's claws; it was the Romans who made them into scales. The Arabic names of its stars still speak of “claws”.
histoires.capricorne: A goat with a fish's tail, very old: the Babylonians already drew it. The Greeks saw the god Pan, who turned half into a fish to escape the monster Typhon. It is one of the oldest figures in the sky.
histoires.verseau: A young man pouring water from a jar. For the Greeks he was Ganymede, cupbearer to the gods, who served them drinks on Mount Olympus. His stars are faint, in a region of the sky full of watery figures.
histoires.poissons: Two fish tied together by a cord. Aphrodite and her son Eros turned into fish to escape the monster Typhon, and tied themselves together so as not to lose each other. Today, the Sun stands here at the start of spring.
histoires.ophiuchus: A man holding a serpent. He is Asclepius, the god of medicine, so gifted that he could bring the dead back to life. The serpent coiled around a staff is still the symbol of doctors.
histoires.lievre: A hare hiding at the feet of the hunter Orion, chased by his dog. Orion loved hunting hares. Its stars are easy to find, just below the great figure of Orion.
histoires.baleine: The sea monster sent by Poseidon to devour Andromeda. Perseus turned it to stone by showing it Medusa's head. Here lies Mira, “the amazing one”, a star that appears and fades over the months.
histoires.hydre: The largest constellation in the sky: a long water snake. For the Greeks it is the Lernaean Hydra, whose heads grew back, slain by Heracles. It is also seen as the snake of Apollo's crow, with the Cup and the Crow on its back.
histoires.coupe: The cup of Apollo. The crow was supposed to bring back water in it, but dawdled on the way. The Cup and the Crow sit on the back of the Hydra.
histoires.colombe: Noah's dove, which flew back to the ark with an olive branch. Scholars of the late 16th century added it to the sky. It flies near Canis Major.
histoires.eridan: A long river of stars flowing south. Phaethon, son of the Sun, lost control of the Sun's chariot and fell into this river. It ends with Achernar, “the end of the river”.
histoires.centaure: Chiron, the wisest of the centaurs, half man and half horse. He was the teacher of heroes such as Achilles and Jason. It holds the stars closest to the Sun, just over 4 light-years away.
histoires.carene: The keel of the ship Argo, which carried Jason and the Argonauts in search of the golden fleece. The great ship was split into three in the 18th century: Carina, Puppis and Vela. It holds Canopus, the second brightest star in the sky.
histoires.voiles: The sails of the ship Argo, on which Jason set out to find the golden fleece. Together with Carina and Puppis, they once formed a single huge constellation. The astronomer Lacaille divided it into three in the 18th century.
histoires.poupe: The stern of the ship Argo, the Argonauts' boat. Jason and his companions, including Heracles and Orpheus, sailed to the edge of the known world. It is the northernmost part of the old great ship.
histoires.loup: A wild animal held by the Centaur, who seems to offer it on the nearby Altar. The Greeks did not say which beast it was; it became a wolf in the Renaissance. The Babylonians already saw a wild dog here.
histoires.autel: The altar on which the gods of Olympus swore to stay united before their war against the Titans. Zeus then placed it in the sky. On old star maps, its flames rise towards the south.
histoires.couronneaustrale: A wreath of leaves at the feet of Sagittarius. According to one Greek story, Dionysus placed it in the sky after bringing his mother back from the Underworld. Its stars form a pretty arc.
histoires.triangleaustral: A triangle of bright stars, the southern twin of the northern Triangle. Dutch navigators added it to the sky in the late 16th century, while crossing the southern seas.
histoires.paon: A peacock, the bird whose feathers are decorated with eyes. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century. The Greeks said the goddess Hera put the hundred eyes of the giant Argus on the peacock's tail.
histoires.grue: A long-necked crane, a marsh bird. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century. Its stars draw a bird in flight, wings spread.
histoires.phenix: The phoenix, the legendary bird that rises from its own ashes. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century. Before them, the Arabs saw a boat in these stars.
histoires.poissonaustral: A big fish drinking the water poured by Aquarius. For the Greeks it was the parent of the two Fishes. Its mouth is Fomalhaut, a bright, lonely star of the autumn sky.
histoires.toucan: A toucan, the South American bird with a big colourful beak. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century. It holds the Small Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of ours.
histoires.mouche: A fly, the only constellation that shows an insect. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century; at first it was called the Bee. It lies just below the Southern Cross.
histoires.hydremale: A small water snake, not to be confused with the great Hydra. Dutch navigators added it to the southern sky in the late 16th century. It slips between the two Magellanic Clouds.
